html:
Tickets for a concert go on sale at 10:00. There are 100 seats, and 20,000 people are waiting with their finger on the button. The design question:

How do you make sure you never sell more seats than you have, and never sell the same seat twice, while thousands of people buy at the same time?

The same problem shows up everywhere: the last item in stock, a hotel room, a doctor's appointment, a limited coupon. It's one of the best ways to show you understand concurrency in an interview, because the naive code looks right and passes every test, until real traffic arrives.

The Naive Version

@Transactional
public void buy(long productId) {
    Product product = products.findById(productId);
    if (product.getStock() < 1) {
        throw new SoldOutException();
    }
    product.setStock(product.getStock() - 1);
    products.save(product);
}

Read the stock, check it, write it back. Now two buyers arrive at the same moment, with one item left:

Time Buyer A Buyer B Stock in the database
1 Reads stock: 1 1
2 Reads stock: 1 1
3 1 ≥ 1, writes stock 0 0
4 1 ≥ 1, writes stock 0 0

Both checks passed, both buyers paid, and the stock says 0. Two items sold, one existed. This is a lost update: B's write is based on a value that A had already changed.

@Transactional doesn't help. Under the default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, both transactions can read the same row, and the database doesn't know that the value you write depends on the one you read. The check and the update must happen as one atomic step, or the row must be protected between them.

There are four good ways to do that. Which one fits depends on what you sell.

Fix 1: An Atomic Conditional Update

For a simple counter, let the database do the check and the update in one statement:

UPDATE products
SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE id = :id AND stock >= 1;

The database locks the row while it updates it, so two of these can't run on the same row at once. The second one waits, then sees the new stock, 0, and the WHERE no longer matches. So you only need to check how many rows changed:

@Transactional
public void buy(long productId) {
    int updated = jdbc.update(
        "UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1",
        productId);
    if (updated == 0) {
        throw new SoldOutException();
    }
    orders.save(new Order(productId));
}
  • Pros: one statement, no extra round trip, and no lock held longer than the update. The best choice for quantities.
  • Cons: the rule must fit in a WHERE clause.

Add a constraint as a safety net, so even a bug elsewhere can't push the stock below zero:

ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT stock_not_negative CHECK (stock >= 0);

Fix 2: A Pessimistic Lock

When the decision needs more than a WHERE clause (a maximum of 4 tickets per customer, a price that depends on what's left, several rows to check), lock the row before reading it:

SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = :id FOR UPDATE;

FOR UPDATE locks the row until the transaction ends. Another buyer's SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the same row waits until the first transaction commits, then reads the new stock. The naive code becomes correct:

public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) // SELECT … FOR UPDATE
    @Query("select p from Product p where p.id = :id")
    Product findByIdForUpdate(long id);
}
  • Pros: any logic you like between the read and the write.
  • Cons: buyers of the same product wait in line, one at a time. Keep these transactions short, and never hold the lock while calling a slow service, like a payment provider. When you lock several rows, always lock them in the same order (by id, for example), or two transactions can each wait for the other forever: a deadlock.

Fix 3: Optimistic Locking With a Version

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely. When they're rare, it's cheaper to let everyone read freely and detect a conflict when writing. Add a version column:

@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id
    private Long id;
    private int stock;

    @Version
    private long version;
}

JPA now writes the update like this:

UPDATE products SET stock = 0, version = 8
WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7;

If someone else changed the row since you read it, the version is no longer 7, no row matches, and JPA throws an OptimisticLockException. Catch it and retry the whole operation a few times, reading the fresh stock each time.

  • Pros: no waiting, no locks held; great when two people rarely change the same row, like editing a profile or an article.
  • Cons: under heavy contention, like 20,000 people buying the same product, most attempts fail and retry, and the retries add even more load. Optimistic locking is the wrong tool for a flash sale.

Fix 4: A Unique Constraint for Things With an Identity

Concert seats aren't a quantity: seat F12 either belongs to someone or it doesn't. Model each seat as a row, and let a unique constraint settle who gets it:

CREATE TABLE seat_bookings (
  event_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  seat       TEXT   NOT NULL,
  order_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat)
);

Two buyers insert the same (event_id, seat): the first succeeds, and the second gets a unique violation, which you turn into "Sorry, this seat was just taken." The database guarantees it, whatever the code, the number of servers or the isolation level. The same trick stops double bookings of hotel rooms per night, or appointments per time slot.

Holding a Seat While the Customer Pays

Payment takes time: the customer types a card number, confirms with their bank, maybe gives up. You can't hold a database lock for minutes, and you don't want to sell a seat and then find out the payment failed.

The answer is a reservation with an expiry:

CREATE TABLE reservations (
  id         UUID        PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
  seat       TEXT        NOT NULL,
  status     TEXT        NOT NULL, -- 'held', 'confirmed' or 'released'
  expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

-- At most one active reservation per seat.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_reservation
ON reservations (event_id, seat)
WHERE status IN ('held', 'confirmed');
  1. Hold: when the customer picks a seat, insert a held reservation that expires in 10 minutes. The partial unique index makes sure no one else can hold or buy the same seat.
  2. Pay: the customer pays, with the reservation id as the payment's idempotency key.
  3. Confirm: when the payment succeeds, set the status to confirmed, but only if it's still held: UPDATE … SET status = 'confirmed' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'held'.
  4. Release: a scheduled job sets expired held reservations to released, which frees the seat for the next buyer.

There's one tricky case: the payment succeeds just after the hold expired and the seat went to someone else. The WHERE status = 'held' makes the confirmation fail, so you refund automatically. The rule: check the hold when you confirm, never only when you start.

For quantities instead of seats, the same idea works with the atomic update: move one unit from stock to reserved when the customer starts paying, and move it back if the hold expires.

When One Row Gets Too Hot

All the fixes above serialize the buyers of one product on one row. That's fine for hundreds of sales per second. For a huge flash sale, a single row becomes the bottleneck, so you take the pressure off it:

  • Gate the traffic in Redis. Keep the stock in a Redis counter too, and DECR it first: Redis handles a huge number of these per second. If the result is below zero, answer "sold out" right away without touching the database. Only the requests that got a unit go on to the database, which stays the source of truth.
  • Split the stock. Store 1,000 units as 10 rows of 100, and have each buyer take a unit from a random row. That's 10 times less contention, at the cost of a little bookkeeping when the rows run out unevenly.
  • Queue the orders. Accept purchase requests into a queue and process them in order with a few workers, telling customers "you're in line". It's slower for each customer, but fair, and the database load stays flat whatever the traffic.

Every Failure, and What Happens

What goes wrong What happens Result
Two buyers take the last item at once The conditional update matches for only one of them One sold, one "sold out"
Two buyers pick the same seat The unique constraint rejects the second insert One booking
A bug tries to make the stock negative The CHECK constraint rejects it The stock stays at 0 or more
A customer holds a seat and never pays The hold expires and a job releases it The seat goes back on sale
The payment succeeds after the hold expired The confirmation's WHERE status = 'held' fails Automatic refund, no double sale
The payment request is retried The reservation id is the payment's idempotency key Charged once
20,000 buyers hit one product Redis turns most away; the database handles the rest one at a time The database stays up

The Answer in Short

  1. Never read, check, then write in separate steps: two buyers can pass the check together.
  2. For a quantity, use an atomic conditional update (WHERE stock >= 1) and check the number of rows changed, with a CHECK (stock >= 0) safety net.
  3. For complex rules, lock the row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE and keep the transaction short. For rare conflicts, use a version column and retry.
  4. For things with an identity, like seats, let a unique constraint decide who gets them.
  5. While the customer pays, hold the item with an expiry, confirm only if the hold is still valid, and release expired holds.
  6. For flash sales, take the pressure off the hot row: a Redis gate, split stock, or a queue.
